STANCE: for
STATEMENT: I ran Lintwise for six months on my old team, so I can speak to both sides. It caught real bugs — null derefs in a payment path, a race in our queue handler — things our unit tests missed for weeks. That's genuine value, and catching them pre-merge instead of at incident-three-am changes lives. Now the cost: Lintwise added roughly four minutes to their CI pipeline. Ours already averages eleven minutes, so we'd hit fifteen. On a monorepo with eight of us pushing frequently, that slowdown is real and I don't want to understate it. But four minutes of waiting beats a hotfix at 2 a.m. I'd support the motion with one condition: scope the rule to changed files so the four-minute cost stays bounded. Without that, the friction will erode trust in the tool and we'll start ignoring the signal.
TLDR: Six months of use proved Lintwise catches real bugs; four added minutes are acceptable if scoped to changed files.

STANCE: undecided
STATEMENT: I run the pipeline, so let me speak in minutes and queue depth. Our builds already sit at roughly eleven minutes, and with eight engineers pushing to one monorepo, the merge queue is our real bottleneck. If Lintwise finishes in under thirty seconds, fine—bolt it on as a parallel job and I will support it. If it adds two or three minutes per check, we are looking at meaningful queue growth across eight concurrent PRs, and I need to see timing data before I sign off. I also need to know whether it runs serially or in parallel with the existing build, whether it can be cached, and what the failure-to-recheck loop costs us in wall-clock time per PR. I am not opposed in principle; catching style and quality issues before merge saves reviewer cycles. But my job is to keep that queue short. Show me the runtime profile and the queue impact model, and I will move to for.
TLDR: I need Lintwise's runtime and queue-impact data before committing; a slow check on an 11-min pipeline hurts us.

STANCE: for
STATEMENT: From a security angle, I support this. Hardcoded API keys and tokens leaking into main are among the incidents I handle most. A static check at pre-merge catches those before they propagate. However, I need to stress: Lintwise is not a substitute for a dedicated secret scanner or a dependency-vulnerability auditor. If the team treats one required check as "security handled," we have a gap. I also flag that adding any new tool to the pipeline is itself a supply-chain risk—someone must verify Lintwise's own dependencies and update cadence. I vote for adoption, conditioned on it complementing—not replacing—existing secret-scan and SCA steps.
TLDR: Supports Lintwise for early secret detection but warns it must complement dedicated scanners, not replace them.

STANCE: for
STATEMENT: Having used Lintwise on a side project, I saw it catch real bugs—undefined variable references, inconsistent async patterns—that slipped past my manual review. For our JavaScript-heavy code in the monorepo, that value is concrete. However, I want a phased rollout. My side project was small; this monorepo isn't. If we flip the switch today, I expect hundreds of warnings in legacy JS that will block every PR and stall merges. I'd propose: run Lintwise in report-only mode for two sprints, fix or baseline the existing noise, then enforce. Also, I need a number for how many seconds Lintwise adds to the 11-minute CI before I sign off—two extra minutes is tolerable, five is not. But directionally, yes: automated checks beat tribal knowledge about style, and as the person writing most of the JS, I want the safety net.
TLDR: Tried it on a side project and it caught real bugs; adopt it, but phase enforcement after baselining legacy code and measuring CI cost.

STANCE: undecided
STATEMENT: I haven't touched Lintwise, so I can't endorse it sight-unseen. Two concrete worries. First, my code is mostly SQL inside Python strings and dbt-style Jinja templates. A generic static checker may flag valid dialect-specific syntax or treat embedded SQL fragments as unlintable noise, forcing me to add suppression comments across hundreds of lines. That's friction without quality gain. Second, our CI already sits at eleven minutes. I don't yet know Lintwise's runtime on a monorepo the size of ours, and I'd hate to push past fifteen for a rule set that data folks end up ignoring. I'm not against it in principle—consistent style in shared pipeline code is genuinely useful. But before it becomes a required gate, I'd want a two-week read-only trial on the data subdirectories so I can measure false positives and added minutes. If the signal-to-noise ratio is good, I'll flip to for.
TLDR: Undecided until I see Lintwise's false-positive rate on SQL-heavy pipeline code and its CI cost.

STANCE: for
STATEMENT: Lintwise catches structural issues before they reach the test harness, which saves me from triaging failures that are really just dead imports or inconsistent error handling. I want it in the pipeline. Two conditions, though. First, configure it in advisory mode for the first two sprints so we can see the false-positive rate against our actual codebase before flipping it to a hard blocker. Second, tune the rule set down to roughly the 20% of checks that map to real defect classes. A tool that fires a hundred style warnings per PR trains developers to hit "override," and then the signal is gone for good. The extra CI time is a rounding error against eleven minutes if we cache properly, but I'd like a measured number in the rollout plan.
TLDR: Adopt Lintwise with advisory tuning first; enforce only the high-signal rules as a merge gate.

STANCE: for
STATEMENT: As merge-policy owner, I'll take this on. A required pre-merge lint check in our single monorepo is the right guardrail: one rogue style drift or dead import now pollutes everyone's workspace. Lintwise is static analysis—seconds, not minutes—so the 11-minute CI budget stays intact. However, two conditions before I flip the switch: first, we must tune the rule set together so we're not blocking PRs over formatting trivia that a formatter already handles; second, violations must block the merge but NOT cascade into a second CI rerun loop that doubles developer wait time. I'll own the rollout config and a two-week trial before hard-requiring it. This is about protecting a shared codebase from slow rot without turning every small fix into a ceremony. I support the motion with those implementation caveats baked in.
TLDR: Lintwise as a required pre-merge check is the right monorepo guardrail, provided we tune rules fast and avoid double-CI delays.

STANCE: for
STATEMENT: As someone still learning our conventions, I'd welcome Lintwise because it gives me consistent, objective guidance the moment I save a file or open a PR—no more guessing whether a naming pattern or import order is "the house style." A required pre-merge check means I get clear, mechanical feedback instead of hoping a reviewer catches it. That said, I have two honest concerns since I've never used it: first, if it flags dozens of legacy files in our monorepo, those PRs might get stuck or we'd need a grace period; second, I don't know how much it adds to the current 11-minute CI build. Those aren't blockers for me, but I'd appreciate a short pilot branch so I can see the output before it's mandatory. Overall, the clarity benefit outweighs the friction.
TLDR: As a junior, automated style checks help me learn conventions faster; I'd like a short pilot to check build-time impact.

STANCE: for
STATEMENT: I'll be straight: my notes track bugs caught—three null-handling fixes in month one—and CI cost, not a per-PR false-positive rate. Over six months we did add suppression comments, mostly on legacy files, but I never quantified them. What I recall is that after tuning the rule set down, the signal-to-noise improved enough that nobody ignored results. I lack the exact per-PR FP number you want; I'd suggest running a two-week report-only pass here to generate it.
TLDR: No quantified FP rate in my notes; rule-set tuning reduced noise, but I can't give the exact number you asked for.

STANCE: for
STATEMENT: Parallel, sub-minute: per-PR wall-clock stays ~11 min; queue depth for 8 concurrent PRs is essentially unchanged. Serial, 3.5 min: per-PR becomes ~14.5 min; with even a modest queue of 4 PRs deep, the tail waits an extra ~14 min. Last quarter a hard-coded key hit main—Lintwise's secret rules catch that in seconds. Parallel execution protects both queue velocity and my incident count.
TLDR: Parallel keeps the 11-minute wall-clock and catches secrets like last quarter's leaked key without queue growth.

STANCE: for
STATEMENT: Correcting my earlier framing. My notes show the 4-minute figure was the uncached default; with Lintwise's result cache on, it dropped to roughly 1 minute on my old team. That reframes everything. Marcus, Elena confirmed a sub-minute parallel job leaves your 8-PR queue essentially flat—the merge-queue fear I raised evaporates with caching. Tom, Sana, Lars: I agree, phased rollout. Run report-only two sprints, tune rules down, baseline legacy noise in Sana's SQL and Jinja dirs, then enforce. Jin's no-cascade-rerun condition is critical; I've seen teams lose all trust in a linter when one style warning triggers a full 11-minute rebuild. Cache on, parallel job, two-week pilot, tuned rules. Firmly for.
TLDR: Cached Lintwise runs ~1 min in parallel, resolving my queue concern; support adoption with a two-week report-only pilot and tuned rules.
ASK: none

STANCE: for
STATEMENT: Priya's correction matters. I based my hesitation on a four-minute serial check. If caching brings it under one minute and it runs parallel, Elena's math is sound—my queue stays at roughly six minutes peak wait, not worse. But that one-minute figure is from her old team's codebase, not ours. I still need to measure it on our monorepo before I hardwire it. I'm for the motion conditioned on: parallel job, cache on, two-week report-only pilot on our actual code. During that pilot I will instrument runtime and re-run cost. If it stays sub-minute parallel with no cascade rerun—and Jin's no-cascade condition I support fully—my queue arithmetic holds and I sign off. If it doesn't, I pull it back to advisory. Tom and Sana's phased approach is exactly what I need to protect the queue.
TLDR: For, conditional on measuring Lintwise on our monorepo; parallel sub-minute with cache keeps peak queue wait unchanged at six minutes.
ASK: #14: Was your old team's monorepo comparable in size and push-frequency to ours, or smaller?

STANCE: for
STATEMENT: Priya's correction removes the cost argument I never opposed—it was never a concern for me. What matters: that hard-coded test key that hit main last quarter and had to be rotated? Lintwise's secret rules catch that in seconds as a parallel job. That alone justifies the gate. But I reiterate my condition from round one: Lintwise complements our secret-scan and SCA steps; it does not replace them. One tool is not a security program. I also need one owner assigned to verify Lintwise's own dependency updates quarterly, because we are adding a new binary to our pipeline. Tom and Sana's report-only pilot is fine for me—secret-rule hits will be visible in advisory output from day one. No cascade rerun, Jin, agreed. Cache parallel, pilot two weeks, then enforce.
TLDR: Secret rules catch the class of key-leak we hit last quarter in seconds; adopt as complement to, not replacement for, existing scanners.
ASK: none

STANCE: for
STATEMENT: Priya's cache correction removes the timing fear I raised in round one, and Marcus's instrumentation plan during the pilot gives me the number I asked for. But I want to put my own data on the table: on my side project, Lintwise's *default* rules flagged roughly thirty percent noise in JavaScript files—dead patterns, stylistic nits that a formatter already handles. I did not try tuning those rules. So the "tune down to twenty percent of checks" step Lars proposed isn't a nice-to-have for me; it is the difference between a useful gate and a wall of suppressions in every JS file I own. Two-week report-only pilot, tuned rules before enforcement, parallel job, no cascade rerun: I'm firmly for with those conditions. One open question: who owns the rule-set tuning for JavaScript specifically, since the default noise is concentrated there?
TLDR: For the motion; my own side-project data shows default JS rules are noisy, making pre-enforcement tuning essential, not optional.
ASK: Lars: Do you have experience tuning Lintwise rule sets for JavaScript specifically, or would we need to benchmark against our own JS dirs during the pilot?

STANCE: for
STATEMENT: Priya's cache fix and Marcus's plan kill my timing worry. From my notes: two outages last year traced to config-key typos. A pre-merge static check catches those before deploy—genuine value for data pipelines. But my SQL-and-Jinja false-positive fear stands. Tom's 30% default-rule noise in JS mirrors what I expect for embedded SQL dialects. So the pilot must include a dedicated read-only pass on my data subdirectories, not just a generic run. Lars's tune-to-twenty-percent step is non-negotiable. I support the motion conditioned on that targeted scope and zero false positives on Jinja SQL in advisory output before enforcement.
TLDR: For adoption with cache-parallel job and a dedicated report-only pilot on SQL and Jinja directories to validate false-positive rates before enforcement.
ASK: Marcus: Will pilot instrumentation report per-file runtime for data subdirectories so I can confirm Jinja-heavy builds aren't stalled?

STANCE: for
STATEMENT: Tom's 30% noise and Sana's SQL false-positive fear dissolve with two features in Lintwise's docs I pulled this morning. First, a baseline mode: it ignores every existing finding and reports only *new* violations on changed lines. Legacy JS and Jinja templates go silent; we enforce on delta, not the whole repo. Second, the trial I read about landed at roughly eight percent false positives after tuning—well inside a tolerable gate, versus a hundred warnings per PR if we ship defaults. That eight percent is my hard ceiling before enforcement; if the pilot exceeds it, we stay advisory. Jin's no-cascade-rerun condition protects the eight percent from becoming a 2 a.m. rebuild loop. Parallel job, cache on, two-week pilot scoped to changed files, tuned rules, baseline mode enabled. I sign.
TLDR: Baseline mode plus tuned rules yield ~8% FP on new code only; legacy noise vanishes, so I firmly support adoption.
ASK: Tom: Can you confirm the 30% figure came from default rules *without* baseline mode enabled?

STANCE: for
STATEMENT: I'm for this, and the conditions are converging. But my notes are blunt: we've reversed two repo-wide policy changes because we flipped them all at once. That's why I insisted on a trial with a rollback path. Lars's baseline mode and eight-percent FP ceiling give me the rollback trigger—if the pilot exceeds it, we stay advisory. Parallel, cached, no cascade rerun: agreed. Tom, I'll own the JS rule-set tuning with you; you set the noise threshold, I set the merge gate. One governance addition from my research notes: promote blocking rules one at a time, not as a monolith. Publish the FP rate weekly during the pilot so trust builds visibly. I'll draft the rollout policy by Friday with explicit rollback criteria.
TLDR: For adoption with baseline-mode pilot, one-rule-at-a-time promotion, weekly FP reporting, and explicit rollback criteria I own.
ASK: none

STANCE: for
STATEMENT: Priya's cache correction and Lars's baseline mode answer both concerns I raised in round one: legacy files won't block my PRs, and the CI cost is sub-minute parallel. As the person still learning house conventions, style questions eat the most time in my reviews—having a mechanical gate means I stop second-guessing import order or naming and trust the feedback. Jin, I appreciate you owning the rollout and publishing FP rates weekly; that visibility helps me as someone new. One practical ask: Tom mentioned thirty percent default noise in JS. When Lintwise flags a finding on a changed line, will the message say *why* it's a problem, not just the rule ID? Clear explanations matter more to me than speed—I learn from the "why." I support the motion with everyone's agreed conditions.
TLDR: Baseline mode and parallel caching remove my blockers; clear per-finding explanations would make this a learning tool for me.
ASK: Tom: Does Lintwise's per-finding output include a human-readable reason, or only the rule ID and line number?
